# Testing a model's calibration yourself {#sec-ch09}

A week after Jev was launched, two opinions were being shared. TypeSafe said Jev gives *calibrated* probabilities [@typesafe2026]. The data scientist Alex Molas replied with a post titled "Jev can't be calibrated". His point was that calibration depends on *your* data, and Jev has never seen your data, so its outputs should be treated as scores, not probabilities [@molas2026]. Who is right? In a precise sense, both are. And you can settle the question for your own use in one afternoon.

::: {.goals}
- Understand why calibration depends on your data.
- Correct a model's numbers when attacks are more or less common at your company.
- Know how many past cases with known answers you need for a fair check.
:::

## Why the critic has a point

Remember from Chapter 2 that a probability tells us how often something happens among similar cases. Now imagine two companies send exactly the same alert to the same model. The model sees the same input, so it gives both companies the same number, say 10%. But suppose one company is attacked often and the other rarely. Then, among alerts like this one, real attacks will be more common at the first company than at the second. The same 10% cannot be correct for both.

This is the base-rate trap from Chapter 2 again, but now it catches the model instead of a person. A model can give correct numbers for one company and numbers that are always too high, or always too low, for another.

::: {.keyidea}
**A model can be right for one company and wrong for yours.** If attacks are rarer at your company than at the companies it learned from, all its numbers will be too high. Always test it on your own past cases.
:::

![The same model's reliability at two companies. At Kestrel, whose mix of alerts matches what the model was tuned for, it sits close to the diagonal. At Harbor, where attacks are rarer, every probability is too high.](/figures/ch18/two-companies.pdf){#fig-two-companies}

To see this, let us imagine a second company, Harbor Pharma. Its alerts come from the same kind of systems and look the same, but real attacks are rarer: {{< num ch18 harbor_base pct1 >}} of alerts, compared with Kestrel's {{< num ch18 kestrel_base pct1 >}}. The same model has a calibration error of {{< num ch18 ece_kestrel f3 >}} at Kestrel, but {{< num ch18 ece_harbor f3 >}} at Harbor, and the error is always in the same direction. Harbor's average predicted risk is {{< num ch18 harbor_mean_p pct1 >}}, while the real rate is {{< num ch18 harbor_base pct1 >}} (@fig-two-companies). The model did not change. Only the situation changed.

## Fixing it

This kind of error is often easy to fix, because it goes in one direction. If you know how common attacks are at your company, you can scale down all the model's odds by the same amount. For example, if attacks are half as common at your company as where the model was tuned, you halve the odds. This is Bayes' rule again [@saerens2002]. If Harbor's base rate is known exactly, its ECE falls to {{< num ch18 ece_prior_known f3 >}}; if the base rate is estimated from 300 labelled alerts, it falls to {{< num ch18 ece_prior_est f3 >}}. **Platt scaling** from Chapter 3, learned from just 300 of Harbor's past alerts with known answers, does even better: {{< num ch18 ece_platt300 f3 >}}.

![Harbor's alerts, on the cases not used for fitting: as returned (red, solid line), after adjusting the odds for Harbor's base rate (blue, dashed line), and after Platt scaling on 300 labelled alerts (green, dotted line). Both fixes bring the curve most of the way back to the diagonal.](/figures/ch18/harbor-fixes.pdf){#fig-harbor-fixes}

Platt scaling also has another advantage: it can fix numbers that are too extreme or not extreme enough, not only numbers that are too high (@fig-harbor-fixes).

## How many labelled cases do you need?

To check a model, we need past cases where we already know the final answer. These are called **labelled cases**, because someone has marked each one as "attack" or "harmless". Collecting them takes people's time, so it is tempting to check with only a few. But a small sample can badly mislead.

![The ECE you'd measure from a random sample of labelled alerts, for different sample sizes, on a model whose ECE over all 20,000 alerts is shown by the labelled black horizontal line. With a hundred labels the measurement is both noisy and too high on average: a calibrated model looks miscalibrated. The error shrinks as samples grow.](/figures/ch18/ece-noise.pdf){#fig-ece-noise}

In our example, the model's real ECE over all 20,000 alerts is {{< num ch18 ece_full f3 >}}. But if we measure it on a random 100 labelled alerts, the typical result is {{< num ch18 ece_n100 f3 >}}, more than three times too high. One time in twenty, it even shows {{< num ch18 ece_n100_hi f3 >}} (@fig-ece-noise). Why does this happen? With only a few cases in each group, the results jump up and down by pure chance, like tossing a coin ten times and getting seven heads. ECE adds up the size of every jump, whether up or down, so chance can only make the error look bigger, never smaller.

::: {.keyidea}
**Testing on too few cases can make a good model look bad.** With only 100 cases, chance alone can make the error look three times bigger than it really is. Use a few hundred cases to correct a model, and a few thousand to be sure.
:::

A simple rule: a few hundred labelled cases are enough to *fix* a big error that always goes in one direction. A few thousand are needed to *prove* that a model's numbers are correct to within one or two percent.

For pick-one questions, start by checking the model's top answer: among the cases where it gave its top option about 80%, was that option correct about 80% of the time? In our example, the top category has an average confidence of {{< num ch18 top_conf_mean pct >}} and is correct {{< num ch18 top_acc pct >}} of the time.

![Top-label calibration for the category question on 2,500 alerts: the confidence of the model's top category against how often that category was right.](/figures/ch18/top-label.pdf){#fig-top-label}

## A routine you can repeat

1. **Collect recent cases whose final answer is now known.** Include a random sample of cases the machine closed by itself; otherwise, you will only have answers for the cases people looked at.
2. **Draw the chart from Chapter 3**, showing how many cases are in each group, and give ECE as a range, not a single number. Look most carefully near the lines where you act.
3. **Check each group separately**: every source, customer type or language that you treat differently.
4. **Fix the problem**: if attacks are simply more or less common at your company, adjust for that; otherwise, use Platt or temperature scaling.
5. **Repeat** this regularly, and whenever the model version or your data changes.

![A testing routine for any model that returns probabilities, Jev included.](/figures/ch18/protocol.pdf){#fig-protocol}

So, the company may be right that Jev is calibrated on the data it tested. The critic is right that this does not prove it is calibrated on yours. This routine turns the argument into a measurement. Until you have done it, treat a new model's outputs as scores, not as probabilities.

::: {.breaks}
Even the "known answers" of past cases are not perfect. Experts sometimes disagree, some attacks are never discovered, and some become clear only later: an alert closed today may turn out to be part of an attack found next month. So test with cases that are old enough for the truth to be known. And remember that cases the model closed by itself were never checked by anyone, so their "answer" is only the model's own guess.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. You have 150 labelled cases and you measure an ECE of 0.05. A colleague says the model is badly calibrated. What would you reply, and what would you do next?
:::
